claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the compared equiatomic quaternary and ternary analogues are single-phase FCC materials.
The quinary alloy's greater chemical complexity promotes a richer diversity of local short-range-order clusters.
Local short-range-order clusters alter the electronic bonding environment at dislocation cores.
The altered bonding environment modifies dislocation-core structures.
Short-range-order-induced dislocation-core modifications facilitate more frequent cross-slip.
More frequent cross-slip enables enhanced dynamic recovery during deformation.
Enhanced cross-slip and dynamic recovery give the quinary alloy superior work-hardening behavior.
Enhanced cross-slip and dynamic recovery delay failure onset in the quinary alloy.
The quaternary and ternary alloys have lower short-range-order density than the quinary alloy.
The quaternary and ternary alloys exhibit fewer cross-slip events than the quinary alloy.
Reduced short-range order in the quaternary and ternary alloys produces more constrained, planar dislocation slip.
The quaternary and ternary alloys have lower yield behavior than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary alloys have lower work-hardening rates than the quinary baseline.
The quaternary and ternary alloys fail earlier than the quinary baseline.
Short-range-order density should correlate quantitatively with cross-slip-event frequency.
APT and high-resolution TEM can quantify and map the relevant local short-range-order features.
The controlled comparison is restricted to identically thermomechanically processed, single-phase FCC alloys deformed at room temperature and approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
Identical thermomechanical histories ensure that all observed variation arises from composition rather than processing history.
